title: Home Responsibility & Independence
subtitle: A chore is a job you were given. Independence is a job you saw.
objectives: Describe the household jobs a Grade 6 student can own
Sequence a task that has waiting built into it
Explain what finishing a job actually means
Explain the difference between a chore and a responsibility
Explain why noticing is the hardest and most valuable skill

cards.title: Somebody is doing all of this right now
cards.text: Meals appear, clothes come back clean, the bin is empty. None of that happens on its own.

cards.title: What each one actually teaches
cards.text: Tap through. The second line is the skill, not the chore.

cards.title: A job with waiting built into it
cards.text: Sort, wash, dry, fold, put away. The waiting between steps is the part people fail, not the work.
points: **Sort by colour** before anything else.
**Wet clothes left in a machine** start to smell.
**Set an alarm** for the end of the cycle.
**Put away is part of the job**, not extra.

question.text: Which part of laundry do people most often fail?
question.explain: Wet clothes left in the drum start to smell. The work is easy; the timing is the skill.

cards.title: A job is done when the tools are away
cards.text: A mechanic who leaves the car running but the bay covered in tools has not finished. The reset is part of the work.
points: **Cooking is not done** until the kitchen is clear.
**Homework is not done** until the desk is clear.
**Leaving the mess** moves the job to someone else.
**Finishing includes the reset.**

question.text: A cooking job is finished when the food is ready.
question.explain: The kitchen has to be reset. Leaving it just moves the rest of the job to somebody else.

cards.title: Halfway
cards.text: Part 2 is the difference between chores and responsibility. Take a moment.

cards.title: Two words that sound the same and are not
cards.text: A chore is assigned to you. A responsibility is something you have taken on and now nobody has to check.

cards.title: From being told to being trusted
cards.text: The moment a job stops needing reminders is the moment it becomes yours, and that changes what people give you.
points: **Reminders mean it is still theirs.**
**No reminders means it is yours.**
**Trust is given for a track record**, not a promise.
**More freedom follows**, in that order.

cards.title: Nobody checks whether you did the roadwork
cards.text: A coach cannot watch your morning run. It shows up in the third round, weeks later, either way.
points: **Unsupervised work** is the work that counts.
**It shows up late**, which is why it is hard.
**Nobody will thank you** at the time.
**Do it anyway.** That is the whole idea.

cards.title: The hardest skill on this list
cards.text: Doing an unassigned job is different in kind from doing an assigned one. It means you looked at the room, not the list.
points: **Anyone can follow instructions.**
**Seeing what needs doing** is rarer.
**Start with one thing a day.**
**Do not announce it.** It counts more quietly.

question.text: What turns a chore into a responsibility?
question.explain: Reminders mean the job is still theirs. No reminders means it has become yours.

cards.title: Everything here is a skill you will need alone
cards.text: In six or seven years, nobody will be doing any of this for you. That is not a threat. It is a timetable.
points: **One meal you can cook** is a real start.
**Your own laundry**, start to finish.
**Learning it now** costs almost nothing.
**Learning it later** costs a lot more.

terms.def: A household job you have been assigned.
A job that is yours, and no longer needs reminding.
Returning a space to how it was. Part of finishing, not extra.
Being able to run your own daily life without supervision.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Waiting is the hard part** of laundry.
**A job is done when the space is reset.**
**No reminders means it is yours.**
**Noticing** is the skill worth building.

quiz.text: What is the correct order for doing laundry?
options: Sort, wash, dry, fold, put away
Wash, sort, fold, dry, put away
quiz.explain: Sorting by colour comes first, and putting away is part of the job rather than extra.
quiz.objective: Sequence a task that has waiting built into it

quiz.text: Why should you set an alarm for the end of a wash cycle?
options: Wet clothes left in the drum start to smell
The machine will not stop otherwise
quiz.explain: The waiting between steps is what people fail, not the work itself.
quiz.objective: Sequence a task that has waiting built into it

quiz.text: Putting clothes away is an optional extra after laundry.
quiz.explain: False. A basket of clean, unfolded clothes is an unfinished job, not a finished one.
quiz.objective: Sequence a task that has waiting built into it

quiz.text: When is a cooking job actually finished?
options: When the kitchen has been reset
When the pan is off the heat
quiz.explain: The reset is part of the work. Leaving it moves the rest of the job to someone else.
quiz.objective: Explain what finishing a job actually means

quiz.text: What does 'reset' mean in this context?
options: Returning a space to the state you found it in
quiz.explain: Same idea as a mechanic putting the tools away. Finishing includes the reset.
quiz.objective: Explain what finishing a job actually means

quiz.text: What is the difference between a chore and a responsibility?
options: A chore is assigned; a responsibility no longer needs reminding
quiz.explain: Reminders mean the job is still theirs. The reminders stopping is the whole shift.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between a chore and a responsibility

quiz.text: Trust is usually given for a track record rather than a promise.
quiz.explain: True. More freedom follows a record of jobs done without reminders, in that order.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between a chore and a responsibility

quiz.text: Which of these builds the skill of working to someone else's deadline?
options: Rubbish out on the right day
quiz.explain: The collection day is set by someone else, and missing it has a visible consequence.
quiz.objective: Describe the household jobs a Grade 6 student can own

quiz.text: What does keeping your own room build?
quiz.explain: A daily reset means the deep clean stays small. That is maintenance rather than rescue.
quiz.objective: Describe the household jobs a Grade 6 student can own

quiz.text: What makes noticing harder than following instructions?
options: You have to look at the room rather than a list
quiz.explain: Anyone can follow instructions. Seeing what needs doing is the rarer skill.
quiz.objective: Explain why noticing is the hardest and most valuable skill

quiz.text: What is a good way to start practising noticing?
options: A full clean once a month
Making a list for someone else
quiz.explain: One a day, and without announcing it. It counts more quietly.
quiz.objective: Explain why noticing is the hardest and most valuable skill

quiz.text: Learning household skills later in life is roughly as easy as learning them now.
quiz.explain: False. Learning them now costs almost nothing. Learning them under pressure later costs much more.
quiz.objective: Explain why noticing is the hardest and most valuable skill

teacher.summary: Week 9 covers household responsibility. The lesson's organising distinction — a chore is assigned, a responsibility no longer needs reminding — gives both of you a shared vocabulary for a conversation that is otherwise easy to have badly. The laundry card is deliberately about the waiting rather than the washing, because for a child with ADHD the failure point in a multi-stage task is almost always the gap, not the work. The 'finishing includes the reset' rule is the single most enforceable idea here, and the boxing card makes the honest case for unsupervised effort without moralising.
discussion: Ask him which jobs at home he currently needs reminding about, and pick one to move across.
Ask what 'finished' means for a job he already does.
Ask what he noticed this week that nobody asked him to do.
Ask which of the six jobs he would most want to own, and let him choose.
teacher.extension: Give him one job for two weeks with no reminders at all, agreed in advance. Whether it works is the lesson either way, and it is worth discussing honestly afterwards.
misconceptions: 'The job is done when the main task is over.' Finishing includes returning the space to how you found it.
'Laundry is hard work.' The work is easy; managing the waiting between stages is the skill.
'Doing chores earns freedom immediately.' Trust follows a track record, which takes weeks.
'Noticing is just being helpful.' It is a distinct skill: looking at the room instead of the list.
